{{Short description|Square tiles used in graphic design}}
In [[information visualization]] and [[graphic design]], '''Truchet tiles''' are square tiles decorated with patterns that are not [[rotational symmetry|rotationally symmetric]]. When placed in a [[square tiling]] of the plane, they can form varied patterns, and the orientation of each tile can be used to visualize information associated with the tile's position within the tiling.<ref name="browne08">{{citation
 | last = Browne | first = Cameron
 | doi = 10.1016/j.cag.2007.10.001
 | issue = 2
 | journal = Computers & Graphics
 | pages = 268–281
 | title = Truchet curves and surfaces
 | volume = 32
 | year = 2008}}.</ref>

Truchet tiles were first described in a 1704 memoir by [[Sébastien Truchet]] entitled "Mémoire sur les combinaisons", and were popularized in 1987 by [[Cyril Stanley Smith]].<ref name="browne08"/><ref>{{citation
 | last = Smith | first = Cyril Stanley | author-link = Cyril Stanley Smith
 | doi = 10.2307/1578535
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[Leonardo (journal)|Leonardo]]
 | pages = 373–385
 | title = The tiling patterns of Sebastian Truchet and the topology of structural hierarchy
 | volume = 20
 | year = 1987| jstor = 1578535 }}. With a translation of Truchet's text by Pauline Boucher.</ref>

==Variations==
===Contrasting triangles===
The tiles originally studied by Truchet are split along the diagonal into two triangles of contrasting colors. The tiles have four possible orientations.

[[File:Truchet base tiles bordered.png|center]]

Some examples of surface filling made tiling such a pattern.

===Quarter-circles===
A second common form of the Truchet tiles, from {{harvtxt|Smith|1987}}, decorates each tile with two quarter-circles connecting the midpoints of adjacent sides. Each such tile has two possible orientations.

{{multiple image
| align     = center
| footer    = 
| width     = 120
| image1    = Truchet tile.svg
| alt1      = Truchet tile
| caption1  = The Truchet tile
| image2    = Truchet tile inverse.svg
| alt2      = Truchet tile inverse
| caption2  = Inverse of the Truchet tile, created by any 90° rotation or orthogonal flip
}}

We have such a tiling:

[[File:Truchet tiling.svg|thumb|center|250px]]

This type of tile has also been used in abstract strategy games [[Trax (board game)|Trax]] and the [[Black Path Game]], prior to Smith's work.<ref name="browne08"/>

===Diagonal===
A [[labyrinth]] can be generated by tiles in the form of a white square with a black diagonal. As with the quarter-circle tiles, each such tile has two orientations.<ref name="goto">{{cite book | url=https://news.mit.edu/2013/10-print-chr2055rnd1-goto-10 | title=10 PRINT CHR$(205.5+RND(1)); : GOTO 10 | publisher=MIT Press | author=Montfort, Nick | year=2012}}</ref>
The connectivity of the resulting labyrinth can be analyzed mathematically using [[percolation theory]] as [[bond percolation]] at the critical point of a diagonally-oriented grid.
[[Nick Montfort]] considers the single line of [[Commodore 64]] [[BASIC]] required to generate such patterns{{snd}} <code>10 PRINT CHR$(205.5+RND(1)); : GOTO 10</code>{{snd}} to be "a [[concrete poetry|concrete poem]], a found poem".<ref name="goto"/>

[[File:Truchet labyrinth.png|center|thumb|250px|A labyrinth generated from diagonal tiles]]
